blocks.text: Edwin Hubble laid the foundation of modern cosmology by showing that galaxies are moving away from the Earth and that their velocity increases with distance: the farther a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away.

blocks.title: Hubble's law
blocks.text: The recession velocity v of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance d from the Earth: v = Ho d (21.5), where Ho is Hubble's constant, about 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1.

Fig 21.6 shows Hubble's law as a straight-line relation between the redshift (recession velocity) of galaxies and their distance from Earth; its slope is the Hubble constant, which measures the rate of cosmic expansion. All galaxies are moving away from each other, and an observer in another galaxy would see the same effect, because space itself is stretching.

blocks.alt: Graph with Recession velocity on the vertical axis and Distance on the horizontal axis. Many dots lie close to a straight line through the origin, with a dense cluster in the middle.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.6: Graphical representation of Hubble's law (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.6).

blocks.text: Scientists often use an inflated-balloon model (Fig 21.7): dots on the surface of a balloon represent galaxies and the skin represents space-time. As the balloon is inflated every dot 'sees' all the other dots moving away. So, wherever we are in the universe, we would see galaxies moving away: the expansion is happening everywhere and there is no special centre; Earth is not at the centre of the universe.

blocks.alt: Three dark balloons of increasing size, each with grid lines and the same light dots at the same places; on the larger balloons the dots are farther apart.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.7: Analogy of the expanding universe: dots move apart as the balloon inflates (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.7).

blocks.text: Since the universe is expanding now, we can conceptually reverse time. This implies that (i) in the past the galaxies were closer together, and (ii) further back, all matter was compressed into a very small, dense and hot state. This idea is the basis of the Big Bang theory, which proposes that the universe began from an initial singularity about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since. Hubble's law provides strong observational evidence that the universe is not static but expanding, and is one of the key pillars of the Big Bang model. Fig 21.8 shows an approximate timeline of the universe from the Big Bang to the present.

blocks.alt: A cone widening upwards from the Big Bang at the bottom. Stages up the cone with times: Big Bang, 0; Recombination Era, 380 thousand years; First stars appear, 300 million years; Early galaxies, 1 billion years; Modern galaxies (Acceleration), Today. Small labels: First structure formation; Expanding proto-clusters; Current Era: Lambda-CDM, with arrows showing galaxies moving apart.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.8: Approximate timeline of the universe's evolution from the Big Bang to present (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.8).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Before Hubble's discovery, most scientists thought the universe was static. Hubble's law turned that idea on its head, suggesting that the universe had a beginning and leading to the Big Bang theory.

Satellite remote sensing uses sensors aboard orbiting spacecraft to monitor and analyse Earth's environment from space. It lets scientists track deforestation, climate change, ocean temperatures and atmospheric composition. Unlike ground-based methods, it offers wide geographic coverage and repeated observations over time, making long-term environmental monitoring possible (Fig 21.9).

blocks.alt: The Sun (Energy source) shines on the Earth (Target). Rays from the Earth go up to a satellite (Sensor), passing a point where radiation is scattered in all directions. The satellite sends signals down to a dish and buildings (Processing station); a thick arrow carries the data to a person at a computer (Analysis), and then to a laptop showing a coloured map (Application).
blocks.caption: Figure 21.9: The remote sensing process (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.9).

items: Source and illumination: the first element is a source that illuminates the target with electromagnetic radiation.
Atmosphere: the radiation interacts with the atmosphere on its way, by scattering, reflection and so on.
Interaction with the target: the radiation interacts with the target; the interaction depends on the properties of the target and the radiation.
Recording with a sensor: the emitted or reflected radiation is recorded by a sensor that is remote (not in contact with the target).
Transmission and reception: the recorded data are transmitted to a receiving station and converted into a usable form such as images.
Interpretation and analysis: the processed image is interpreted, electronically or digitally, to obtain information.
